note.question: When can an online retailer and its offline competitor both gain by letting online customers return products at the offline store, and how does the agreement alter price competition?
note.overview: Competing online and offline retailers simultaneously choose prices under no agreement and under a buy-online-return-in-store arrangement. Forward-looking consumers choose purchase, return, and repurchase paths, and the retailers' agreement and transfer-payment incentives are analyzed in equilibrium.

components.label: Information structure
components.explanation: Consumers know prices and rationally anticipate mismatch probability and all later return and repurchase costs. An online product's nondigital match is learned only after delivery; an offline shopper can inspect before purchase. After a mismatch, the consumer learns which remaining variant will match, so a second purchase does not mismatch. Retailers anticipate consumers' full decision paths when choosing prices.

components.label: Pure-strategy retail-price equilibrium with endogenous consumer return paths
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Pure-strategy retail-price equilibrium with endogenous consumer return paths. The authors solve consumers' sequential decisions for any price pair and substitute the resulting demands into simultaneous retailer profit maximization. Lemma 2 characterizes two pure-strategy BORS equilibria, and the agreement analysis compares these with the unique no-agreement equilibrium.

It is only when the online retailer relinquishes returners that the competition alleviation effect can lead to a higher offline price (which happens when θp < θ ≤θ2).
